lessons.title: Two halves, no stopping
lessons.objective: You can explain how long a match is and why the clock does not stop.

payload.prompt: How long is a football match?

explanation.correct: Right. Two halves of 45 minutes each, plus the referee adds stoppage time at the end.
explanation.incorrect: It's 90 minutes total: two 45-minute halves. The clock never actually stops though, so there's extra time added.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ninety minutes is what they call regulation time.

payload.prompt: Guess: how many extra minutes did the ref add today?

explanation.correct: Close. Refs typically add between three and eight minutes per half for injuries, goals and delays.
explanation.incorrect: Typically three to eight minutes depending on how much time was lost to injuries and celebrations.
explanation.sayThisLine: Six added on and there's still two minutes of injury time coming.

lessons.title: What counts as a goal
lessons.objective: You can tell a goal from a near miss by the whole-ball-over-the-line rule.

payload.prompt: The whole ball crossed the line between the posts, no bounce before. Goal?

scene.alt: The ball is played forward and the whole ball crosses the goal line between the posts at waist height.

explanation.correct: Yes. When the whole ball crosses the whole line, it's a goal.
explanation.incorrect: If the whole ball crosses the whole line between the posts and under the crossbar, it is a goal.
explanation.sayThisLine: Whole ball over the line, that's a goal.

payload.prompt: Half the ball is over the line. Is it a goal?

options.text: No, the whole ball must cross
Only if a player touched it

explanation.correct: Correct. The whole ball must completely cross the whole line for it to count.
explanation.incorrect: The whole ball has to fully cross for it to count. A half-ball situation is not a goal.
explanation.sayThisLine: The whole ball, the whole line. That's the rule.

lessons.title: Getting the ball back into play
lessons.objective: You can say who restarts play after the ball goes out.

payload.prompt: Match the restart to what caused it.

pairs.definition: Attacker put it over the touchline; the opponent restarts with hands over head.
Attacker put it over the goal line; the defending goalkeeper or defender restarts from the six-yard box.
Defender put it over their own goal line; attacker restarts from the corner arc.

explanation.summary: Who touched it last and which line it crossed decides the restart.
explanation.sayThisLine: Ball goes out, the other team restarts it.

payload.prompt: Tap the corner arc, where corner kicks are taken.

diagram.alt: A full pitch with the corner arc highlighted at each corner.

explanation.correct: Right. A corner is taken from the arc in the corner, and you can score straight from it.
explanation.incorrect: The corner arc is a small quarter-circle in each corner, where the ball is placed for a corner kick.

payload.prompt: The ball goes out off a defender's foot. Who restarts it?

explanation.correct: Right. The team that did NOT touch the ball last restarts it.
explanation.incorrect: The attacking team restarts because the defending team put it out.
explanation.sayThisLine: Out off them, so we get the restart.

lessons.title: Free kicks and penalties
lessons.objective: You can explain direct vs indirect free kicks and when a penalty is given.

diagram.alt: The attacking third showing the penalty area, six-yard box, and penalty spot.

explanation.correct: Right. A foul inside this area is a penalty kick.
explanation.incorrect: The penalty area is the larger rectangle; the six-yard box is inside it. Fouls in the penalty area are penalties.

payload.prompt: A defender deliberately holds an attacker. Direct or indirect free kick?

scene.alt: A holding foul in the middle of the pitch. The attacker is held by the shoulder.

explanation.correct: Direct. A holding foul is a direct free kick, so the shooter can score straight from it.
explanation.incorrect: Dangerous contact like holding, pushing or dangerous play is a direct free kick. You can score straight from it.
explanation.sayThisLine: That's a direct foul, he can just shoot it in.

options.text: A foul anywhere on the pitch
A foul by a defender in their penalty area
A foul by an attacker in their own half

explanation.correct: Exactly. A foul inside the defender's penalty area is a penalty kick from 12 yards.
explanation.incorrect: A foul by the defending team inside their own penalty area gives a penalty kick.
explanation.sayThisLine: Foul in the box, that's a penalty.

lessons.title: Points, tables and drama
lessons.objective: You can read a league table and explain what a win, draw and goal difference do.

payload.template: A win gets {{win}} points, a draw gets {{draw}}, and a loss gets {{loss}}.

explanation.correct: Right. Three for a win, one for a draw, zero for a loss. The table ranks teams by points.
explanation.incorrect: Three points for a win, one for a draw, none for a loss.

payload.prompt: Two teams have the same points. What breaks the tie?

options.text: Goal difference (goals for minus goals against)

explanation.correct: Right. Goal difference is the first tiebreaker in most leagues.
explanation.incorrect: When teams have the same points, goal difference (how many more they scored than conceded) is the first tiebreaker.
explanation.sayThisLine: Same points but we're third because our goal difference is better.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: Fourth clean sheet in a row, that back line is locked in.

payload.question: What does 'clean sheet' mean?

options.text: A fresh team sheet for the new season
A match with no goals allowed

payload.translation: Her team hasn't let in a goal in the last four matches; the defence is playing well.

followUps.line: Is the goalkeeper getting a lot of action?
followUps.why: Shows you know defences need support.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If you don't watch often, ask who's playing well lately.

lessons.title: Knockouts, extra time and shootouts
lessons.objective: You can follow a knockout tie, including two-legged ties and shootouts.

payload.prompt: Order the knockout tiebreak from start to finish.

items.why: Two halves of 45 minutes plus stoppage time.
Two 15-minute periods if level after 90 minutes.
Alternating penalties if still level after extra time.
If level after five each, one miss decides it.

explanation.correct: That is the path: 90 minutes, then 30 of extra time, then five penalties each, then sudden death.
explanation.incorrect: First 90 minutes, then two 15-minute periods of extra time, then a shootout with five penalties each, then sudden death.
explanation.sayThisLine: It went to sudden death and they finally scored.

payload.prompt: A two-legged tie: first leg 2-1, second leg 1-1. Who goes through?

options.text: It's 3-2 on aggregate, so the first team

explanation.correct: Right. It's 3-2 on aggregate (combined score), so the first team advances.
explanation.incorrect: You add the goals from both legs. If it's level on aggregate, extra time and penalties are played.
explanation.sayThisLine: It's 3-2 on aggregate so they're through.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: It'll go to penalties, I can't watch.

payload.question: What does she mean?

options.text: The match is being decided by individual penalty kicks
The referee will give out a lot of yellows
Extra time is about to start

payload.translation: After extra time, if it's still level, both teams take five penalty kicks each to decide it. She's nervous.

followUps.line: How many does each team get before sudden death?
Is your keeper good at penalties?
followUps.why: Asks a genuine question about her team's strength.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You can say you find shootouts stressful too.

lessons.title: Eleven, the bench and the armband
lessons.objective: You can explain who plays, how substitutions work and what a captain does.

payload.prompt: How many players start on the pitch per team?

explanation.correct: Right. Eleven on the pitch at the start: one goalkeeper and ten outfield players.
explanation.incorrect: Each team starts with 11 players on the pitch.
explanation.sayThisLine: Eleven on the pitch, and five subs they can use.

payload.template: Modern football allows up to {{num}} substitutions per match in {{windows}} windows, plus half-time.

explanation.correct: Right. Five subs in three windows: one before the game, one at half-time, and one after.
explanation.incorrect: Five substitutions across three tactical windows (typically one before half-time, at half-time, and in the second half).

lessons.title: Scoring milestones fans cheer
lessons.objective: You can use hat-trick and brace correctly and know the fan talk around them.

payload.prompt: Match the scoring term to its meaning.

pairs.definition: Two goals scored by one player in a single match
Three goals scored by one player in a single match
Four goals by one player, a rarer achievement

explanation.summary: These terms celebrate individual goal-scoring feats in a single match.
explanation.sayThisLine: He got a brace in the first half and finished with a hat-trick.

statement.speaker: Maya
statement.text: He got a hat-trick in the first half, absolutely ridiculous.

payload.question: What is she talking about?

options.text: A hat passed to him three times

payload.translation: One player scored three goals in just the first 45 minutes, which is exceptional.

followUps.why: Shows genuine surprise at the rarity.

followUps.line: What did the team do in the second half?

payload.noFakeExpertNote: If it's unfamiliar, ask if that's a rare thing.
